days.concept: Codeforces is returning 502 on the API and is unreachable in the browser, so there are no statements and no submissions tonight. That removes the problem set but not the reason day 23 exists. Every core problem planned for today — 1676G, 1830A, 1167C — needed the same prerequisite: a rooted tree held as arrays, with one order in which every parent precedes its children. Tonight builds that prerequisite from memory and proves it correct against a brute force, which needs no network at all. The problem set moves to day 24.
days.watchFor: You are writing five functions with no recursion anywhere. The measured fact behind that rule: at Python's default limit of 1000 a recursive subtree pass on a 200000-node path raises RecursionError, which Codeforces reports as a runtime error, not a wrong answer. Raising the limit does survive on this machine, so the trap is not that recursion always crashes — it is that the default kills you and the iterative version has no ceiling to manage. Build the order first, then every subtree question is one loop over it reversed.

Trees is the thing being walked around, and it is also the blind spot with 0 solves at 1300+ that cost you 2257C in a live round. Today is its second scheduling. There will not be a third. || TODAY'S ONE IDEA: a rooted tree is two arrays and an order, and the order is the whole trick. Hold the tree as parent[v] plus a list `order` in which every vertex appears after its parent. Once you have that, every subtree question is ONE LOOP over order reversed — each vertex is finished before its parent is read, so size[p] += size[v] just works — and every root-downward question is one loop over order forward, because the parent is always already settled. No DFS, no recursion, no searching. Build the order once and the two core problems collapse into a few lines each. || WHY NOT RECURSION, measured rather than assumed: at Python's default limit of 1000, a recursive subtree pass on a 200000-node path raises RecursionError, which Codeforces reports as a RUNTIME ERROR, not a wrong answer. Raising the limit does survive on this machine, so the trap is not that recursion always dies — it is that the default kills you and the iterative version has no ceiling to manage at all. Write the loop. || THE TOOLKIT IS 20 MINUTES AND IT COMES FIRST, before either tree problem. Fill in build_adj, root_tree, subtree_sizes and depths in 20AUG26/toolkit.py and run `python3 testing/check_toolkit.py --core`. It checks you against an independently written brute force and finishes with a 200000-node path. Do not skip it and then improvise inside 1830A — improvising the tree representation is exactly what stalled 2257C. || FOUR PROBLEMS ARE SEALED (1613C, 1366B, 1372B, 1520E). Their tags are withheld. Write ONE LINE naming the technique and why BEFORE any code. That line being wrong is the most useful thing that can happen this morning — the discrimination denominator is only 4 deep and currently reads 2 wrong of 4, and I will ask you for every line at close. || THE GATE IS MANDATORY. Hand me the final file before you submit and I run the samples, an edge battery and a randomised differential check — outside your four hours. Do not write or run gen.py, brute.py or stress.py yourself; that is my job and it costs you no practice minutes. || Submit everything as PyPy 3-64. || NEXT RATED ROUND: Codeforces Round (Div. 2), Saturday 29 August, 20:05 IST, 120 minutes. Eight days out. Rating only moves in rounds and your last three returned +135, +97 and +110 — tell me whether you are playing it so the week points at it.

practice.title: Morning — 4h. Toolkit first, then trees twice.

blocks.label: Mixed opener — tags withheld
blocks.note: Both from topics you have already covered, both sealed, 15 minutes each and the cap is hard. Write ONE LINE naming the technique and why before any code. A wrong line is the data this whole practice order exists to collect; an unfinished problem is not a failure.

problems.name: Poisoned Dagger
problems.why: If you reach for a search, your line must also say what makes the searched quantity monotone. 'binary-search-invariant-unwritten' is severity 5 with five citations.
problems.reveal: Total damage for a given k is sum(min(k, a[i+1]-a[i]) for i in range(n-1)) + k. That total is non-decreasing in k, and THAT is the monotonicity that licenses a search — write it down before you search. Binary search k over [1, h]; k = h always suffices because the final attack alone deals h. Invariant: lo is always insufficient, hi is always sufficient, the answer is hi.

problems.name: Shuffle
problems.why: n and the operation count are both large enough that touching the array once per operation is already too slow, so the shape of the answer is decided before you type.
problems.reveal: Do not simulate the array. The set of positions the single 1 can occupy is ALWAYS a contiguous interval [lo, hi] — that is the invariant, and it holds because if the 1 can reach any position inside an operation's range, one swap moves it to any other position in that range. Start [lo, hi] = [x, x]; for each (l, r), if it intersects [lo, hi] (l <= hi and r >= lo), widen to [min(lo, l), max(hi, r)]; otherwise ignore it. Answer hi - lo + 1, in O(m).

blocks.label: Core — the rooted tree, twice
blocks.note: Do the toolkit first (see the watch-for). These two are deliberately paired: one hands you a valid processing order for free and the other makes you build it. Tags are shown here on purpose — this is the blocked half where you install the technique.

problems.name: White-Black Balanced Subtrees
problems.why: Owed from day 21 and the gentlest possible first use of the toolkit. Before writing anything, answer one question out loud: does this input hand you a valid processing order for free, or must you build one? Then write in a comment what your accumulator stores at index v.
problems.reveal: Map 'W' to +1 and 'B' to -1 and let f[v] be the sum over v's whole subtree. The input guarantees p_i < i, so vertices 1..n are ALREADY in an order where every parent precedes its child — you get `order` for free and need no adjacency list and no DFS at all. One loop v from n down to 2 doing f[p[v]] += f[v] finishes every subtree before its parent is read. Answer is the count of v with f[v] == 0. O(n).

problems.name: Copil Copac Draws Trees
problems.why: The step up, and the reason the toolkit is not optional: the edges arrive in arbitrary order, so nothing is sorted for you and you must build parent and order yourself. Simulating Copil's scans is the trap — 'simulate-instead-of-invariant' is severity 5. Before coding, write one sentence defining a per-vertex quantity that makes the answer a maximum over vertices instead of a loop over passes.
problems.reveal: Keep each edge's position in the input. Root at 1 and define pass[v] = the scan on which v gets drawn: pass[1] = 1, and for v attached to u by the edge at input index idx[v], pass[v] = pass[u] + (1 if idx[v] < idx[u] else 0), taking idx[1] = 0. Within a single scan you can only follow edges of increasing input index; a decrease forces a new scan. Answer is max(pass). Build parent and order with your iterative root_tree, then one forward pass over order. O(n).

blocks.label: Cold re-solve, then debt if there is room
blocks.note: The re-solve is not optional; the debt problem is. Eight cold re-solves are overdue and this is the oldest. Closing five of five beats starting seven — that is the direct lesson of days 21 to 23.

problems.name: Omkar and Last Class of Math
problems.why: Cold re-solve, rep 1 of 2, four days overdue. Blank file, no notes, no old code, do not open your day-13 submission. Before you optimise anything, write down in words the exact quantity your loop returns — that sentence is the entire reason this is on the ladder.
problems.reveal: Minimising lcm(a, b) with a + b = n means making a the LARGEST PROPER DIVISOR of n, not the largest divisor below sqrt(n). Find the smallest divisor d > 1 by scanning to sqrt(n); then a = n // d and b = n - a. For prime n that d is n itself, giving a = 1. Your day-13 sqrt rewrite returned the largest divisor below sqrt(n) instead, and the two quantities first disagree at n = 12.

problems.name: Arranging The Sheep
problems.why: The only open debt, four days old, first reschedule. BONUS ON PURPOSE: start it only once the toolkit and both tree problems are finished. Sealed — name the technique in one line first.
problems.reveal: Collect the sheep positions, then subtract i from the i-th of them, which turns 'adjacent' into 'equal'. Move every normalised value to their median; the sum of absolute deviations is minimised at the median, and that exchange argument is the thing to write down. n is up to 1e6, so read with sys.stdin.buffer, keep the arithmetic integer, and do not build extra lists.

Process v from n down to 2 and add f[v] into f[parent[v]]. Every child is finished before its parent is read. Count vertices with f[v] == 0. O(n), with no adjacency list or traversal needed.

problems.name: Copil Copac Draws Trees
problems.why: The edges arrive in arbitrary order, so this time you must build parent and order. Replace process simulation with one per-vertex state whose maximum is the answer.

Build parent and a parent-before-child order iteratively, process it forward, and return max(pass). O(n).

blocks.label: Mixed opener — tags withheld, four timestamps each
blocks.note: Two covered but different techniques, 15 minutes each. Blank file, no notes and no old code. Before typing, write ONE LINE naming the technique and why the statement licenses it. Record cumulative minutes for understood, chosen, coded and submitted.

problems.name: Interesting drink
problems.why: Cold re-solve, rep 1 of 2, six days overdue after wrong submissions. State exactly what one query asks you to count before choosing any boundary.
problems.reveal: Sort the prices once. For each budget m, bisect_right(prices, m) returns the first index whose price is greater than m; that index is also the number of affordable shops. Boundary invariant: every price left of the returned index is <= m and every price from it onward is > m. O(n log n + q log n).

problems.name: Romantic Glasses
problems.why: Cold re-solve, rep 1 of 2, five days overdue after two TLEs before the AC. Translate the segment condition into one equality before choosing storage.
problems.reveal: Give alternating positions opposite signs and maintain the transformed prefix balance. A segment satisfies the required equality exactly when the same balance appears at two boundaries, so start seen = {0} and answer YES on the first repeated balance. Reset seen per test case. O(n) expected time and O(n) memory.

blocks.label: Debt — third and final scheduling
blocks.note: These are not new volume. Each has already appeared twice and must leave today with a verified verdict or an explicit drop. At the cap, continue only with a concrete hypothesis; otherwise read the editorial once, close it and implement from an empty file.

problems.name: Shuffle
problems.why: Two prior schedules, no attempt. Write the smallest state that can represent every still-reachable answer after an operation; do not touch the whole array per operation.
problems.reveal: The possible positions of the single 1 always form one interval [lo, hi]. Start [x, x]. An operation [l, r] changes nothing when disjoint; when it intersects, every position in the union becomes reachable, so widen to [min(lo, l), max(hi, r)]. Answer hi - lo + 1 in O(m).

problems.name: White-Black Balanced Subtrees
problems.why: Two prior schedules, no attempt. Before code, define the value stored for vertex v and decide whether the input already supplies an order in which its dependencies are ready.
problems.reveal: Map W to +1 and B to -1 and let f[v] be the colour sum of v's whole subtree. The input guarantees parent[v] < v, so n,n-1,...,2 is already child-before-parent: add f[v] to f[parent[v]], then count f[v] == 0. No adjacency list or traversal is needed. O(n).

problems.name: Copil Copac Draws Trees
problems.why: Two prior schedules, no attempt. Replace repeated drawing passes with one state per vertex, then process only after its parent state is ready.
problems.reveal: Store every edge's input index. Root at 1. Let pass[1] = 1 and edge_index[1] = 0. For child v of u, pass[v] = pass[u] + (edge_index[v] < edge_index[u]); a decreasing edge index is exactly where a new scan is forced. Build parent and a parent-before-child order iteratively, process it forward and return max(pass). O(n).

blocks.label: Failed re-solve repair + oldest in-band retention
blocks.note: Blank files and fresh submissions. Do not open an old accepted file. These are re-derivations, not recognition checks; write the objective or predicate before choosing the loop.

problems.name: Omkar and Last Class of Math
problems.why: Yesterday's mixed attempt chose the wrong technique, ran 71 minutes and ended by opening the old AC. Re-derive from lcm(a,b) and test n = 12 before submitting.
problems.reveal: For a + b = n, minimising lcm(a,b) is achieved by taking a as the largest proper divisor of n. Find the smallest divisor d > 1 up to sqrt(n); then a = n // d and b = n - a. If none exists, n is prime and the pair is 1, n-1. The old wrong rewrite is exposed by n = 12.

problems.name: Maximum Median
problems.why: Cold re-solve, rep 1 of 2, six days overdue after a WA before AC. Write the monotone predicate, whether the answer is first-false or last-true, and both boundary meanings before coding.
problems.reveal: Sort a. A candidate x is feasible when sum(max(0, x-a[i]) for i from n//2 to n-1) <= k; lower-half values cannot affect the median. Feasibility is true then false as x rises. Keep lo = a[n//2] feasible and hi = lo+k+1 infeasible, binary-search the last feasible x, and print lo. O(n log n + n log k).
